summary: This note is a long encyclopedic article on lightning, covering its definition as an electrostatic discharge, its cultural and scientific history, and its frequency and distribution worldwide. It explains how thunderstorm electrification separates charge, how leaders, return strokes and re-strikes form a flash, and how the main types (intra-cloud, cloud-to-cloud, cloud-to-ground, positive and negative) differ in physical characteristics and danger.
one_line: Encyclopedic overview of lightning covering its formation, charge separation in thunderstorms, flash mechanics, types, distribution and hazards.
key_facts: Lightning is an electrostatic discharge that temporarily neutralizes two electrically charged regions, releasing an average of between 200 megajoules and 7 gigajoules of energy depending on the type.
Thunder is caused by a shock wave that develops as gases near the discharge experience a sudden increase in pressure.
The main charging area in a thunderstorm occurs in the central part of the storm where temperatures range from −15 to −25 °C (5 to −13 °F).
When rising ice crystals collide with graupel, the ice crystals become positively charged and the graupel becomes negatively charged.
On Earth, lightning frequency is approximately 44 (± 5) times per second, or nearly 1.4 billion flashes per year.
About 70% of lightning occurs over land in the tropics where atmospheric convection is the greatest.
The place where lightning occurs most often is over Lake Maracaibo, where the Catatumbo lightning phenomenon produces 250 bolts of lightning a day.
On April 29, 2020, a bolt 768 km (477.2 mi) long was observed in the southern U.S., according to the World Meteorological Organization.
The first known photograph of lightning is from 1847, by Thomas Martin Easterly.
The first surviving photograph of lightning is from 1882, by William Nicholson Jennings.
The return stroke current averages 30 kiloamperes for a typical negative CG flash, and the core temperature of the plasma may exceed 27,800 °C (50,000 °F).
Cloud-to-ground lightning is the least common but best understood type, and it poses the greatest threat to life and property.
Positive lightning is less common than negative lightning and on average makes up less than 5% of all lightning strikes.
An average bolt of negative lightning carries 30,000 amperes, transfers 15 C of charge and 1 gigajoule of energy, while large positive bolts can carry up to 120 kA and 350 C.
Step potentials from lightning's ground current are responsible for more injuries and deaths in groups of people or animals than the strike itself.
The fear of lightning is called astraphobia.

entities.name: Thomas Martin Easterly
entities.role: Photographer credited with the first known photograph of lightning, from 1847

entities.name: William Nicholson Jennings
entities.role: Photographer who spent half his life capturing pictures of lightning; took the first surviving photograph of lightning, from 1882

entities.name: William Thomson (Lord Kelvin)
entities.role: Demonstrated charge separation in water at the Earth's surface and developed a continuous electric field measuring device

entities.name: Heinz Kasemir
entities.role: First theorized the upward streamer phenomenon

entities.name: World Meteorological Organization
entities.role: Body that reported the 768 km bolt observed on April 29, 2020

entities.name: NASA's Optical Transient Detector
entities.role: Space-based sensor whose data from April 1995 to February 2003 revealed the uneven distribution of worldwide lightning strikes

entities.name: Lake Maracaibo
entities.role: Location where lightning occurs most often, via the Catatumbo lightning phenomenon

entities.name: Catatumbo lightning phenomenon
entities.role: Lightning activity over Lake Maracaibo producing 250 bolts a day on average 297 days a year

entities.name: Kifuka
entities.role: Village in the mountains of the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, second most lightning density on Earth

entities.name: Canyonlands National Park
entities.role: Location in Utah, U.S. of a four-second video of a lightning strike

entities.name: Gulf Stream
entities.role: Warm ocean current whose flow past drier land partially explains elevated lightning frequency in the Southeast United States

entities.name: LOFAR
entities.role: Instrument whose observational data during storms favored a streamer avalanche model of leader initiation

entities.name: Bolt from the blue
entities.role: Lightning strike appearing to initiate from clear sky above an anvil cloud, usually negative in polarity

entities.name: Thundersnow
entities.role: Lightning occurring in the cold of winter, associated with positive lightning
